Subject: Recap & next steps — shared vs dedicated infrastructure (FinPay)

Hey Alex — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap from our call and proposed next steps so we’re aligned: 

What we heard from FinPay:
- Production traffic: steady low-rate requests for fraud scoring (mostly 10–50 req/s) with two daily payroll spikes (~3k reqs over 20–30 minutes).
- Primary concerns: latency SLOs for real-time scoring (P95 goal ~150ms), and noisy-neighbor/resource contention during payroll windows.
- Compliance: logs retention and audit trail requirements — may lean Dedicated or Private if isolation is required.

Our recommendations (high level):
1) Short term: continue on Hosted API for dev & staging; evaluate Dedicated capacity for production payroll windows to guarantee isolation and throughput.
2) Dedicated details: Dedicated GPU pools give you per-tenant compute isolation, prioritized scheduling, and SLA-backed latency/availability targets. We can provide configuration options (reserved slots, burst capacity) to handle the payroll spikes.
3) Private/VPC: if FinPay requires customer-managed networking or specific KMS/HSM controls, Private is the right path — typically a later-stage commitment.

Attachments: I’m including a short SLO and dedicated-capacity overview (redwood-slos-dedicated.pdf) and a high-level prod architecture sketch (prod-architecture.png).

Proposed next steps:
- Share a technical deep-dive with your SREs (can do next Tue or Wed) — Vivek and Marissa from our infra team can run it.
- I’ll follow up with a pricing/commitment preview for a Dedicated pool sized to handle payroll spikes.
- Collect any specific audit/SOC questions from your compliance team so we can route to our security contacts.

Doable to schedule the SRE deep-dive on Tue 2026-05-05 at 10am PT? If not, send two alternatives.

Thanks — talk soon.

— Priyom Das

Great — thanks Alex. Quick answers inline: 

- Isolation guarantees (Dedicated vs Hosted):
  * Hosted: multi-tenant environment with robust resource fairness and automatic throttling. Good for dev and low-volume production, but not SLA-backed per-customer isolation — noisy-neighbor risk exists during extreme bursts.
  * Dedicated: reserved GPU pools that are exclusively allocated to your account. We run per-customer model workers and KV caches; scheduling and preemption policies prioritize dedicated tenants, and you get SLA-backed latency/availability targets. This minimizes noisy-neighbor effects because compute is not shared at the pool level.

- Empirical SLOs: for a payments customer with similar request patterns we consistently delivered P95 < 120–160ms on a Dedicated pool with burst capacity for short spikes; P99 depends on payload sizes and sequence lengths but was typically under 400–500ms with proper batching settings. I’ll send anonymized benchmark excerpts in the deep-dive.

- Pricing/commitment preview: I’ll include a ballpark for a 3-month reserved Dedicated pool capable of handling your peak windows in tomorrow’s follow-up.

Attached: redwood-slos-dedicated.pdf (SLO definitions + example configs).

See you Tue 5/5 10am PT. If your SREs want a short pre-read, point them to the linked doc: https://docs.redwood.com/samples/dedicated-slos

— Priyom

Subject: Technical note: isolation boundaries & noisy-neighbor mitigations

Alex/Priyom — quick technical note ahead of the deep-dive. Attaching a short file (technical-note-isolation.txt) but key points below: 

1) Pool-level isolation: Dedicated capacity maps to dedicated GPU pools (no other tenants share those GPUs). That means scheduling, memory, and PCIe bandwidth are not contended with other customers.
2) Process isolation: within a Dedicated pool we still run per-customer model worker processes; we isolate KV caches per tenant and namespace network egress via VPC routing (for Private deployment we hand this to the customer).
3) QoS controls: we expose prioritized queues and can reserve GPU slots for high-priority real-time traffic (to protect P95).
4) Autoscaling and burst: short-term burst nodes can be pre-warmed and attached to the Dedicated pool; during spikes we avoid noisy neighbors by scaling only within your reserved capacity.
5) Monitoring & SLOs: you get token-level latency histograms, tail latency alerting, and tracing hooks to correlate spikes with workload patterns.

Happy to cover the implementation diagrams on Tue. If there are any infra-level constraints (e.g., strict on-prem segregation or HSM-only key policies), flag them now so we include the right folks.

— Vivek Kulkarni
Principal Infra Engineer | Redwood Inference
